Martin Pistorius Ghost boy

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We speak to Martin Pistorius about his book and his journey to break free from a virtual coma that trapped him in his body for 12 years.

Summary:
Martin Pistorius was a twelve-year-old boy in South Africa when he was struck by a mysterious illness. He was slowly debilitated... until he could no longer move his body, or speak. Then he slipped into what doctors called a vegetative state.

His parents were told he would soon be dead. But after four years, something happened inside Martin. His mind began to function again, but not his body. He was soon fully aware of everything around him, but had no way of sharing. He was trapped inside his own body, like a ghost boy.

But that's far from the end of Martin Pistorius's story. Because today, Martin is speaking again -- albeit with the help of a computer program.

Further information:
Martin Pistorius book, Ghost Boy is taking the world by storm - it's been on the New York Times best Seller list for the last three weeks!

He is currently in South AFrica visiting his family and has agreed to do an interview with Carte Blanche.

Because he speaks through a computer, an interview is quite difficult as we have to provide questions beforehand so there isn't really a natural flow for pick up questions. I suggest that we include the Centre that helped Martin find his "voice". The Centre for Augmentative and Alternative Communication at the University of Pretoria did the initial tests on Martin and proved that he was in fact not in a vegetative state. If it weren't for the centre Martin would still be trapped, living out his years in a care centre watching Barney the Purple Dinosaur.

DEVICE - we can use abstract re-enactments to help tell his story.

Press Release:


Martin Pistorius
Carte Blanche hears exclusively from the ‘Ghost Boy’ - Martin Pistorius - who titled his bestselling book in this way after recovering from a devastating illness that trapped him in a paralysed body for 12 years. Inconceivably, during this time no one suspected that he was aware of every tiny detail of his life.


Script:


GHOST BOY
STUDIO LINK
Best seller NY times list // Met Martin and his family while he was visiting family in South Africa.

SCRIPT
VO: A story of dark days and hopeful moments, Martin Pistorius’ auto-biography, Ghost Boy, has held fast on the New York Times Best Seller list.
MARTIN: Life is truly amazing, I sometimes find it hard to believe, but it’s wonderful.
VO: Unable to physically speak, Martin communicates by using a computer that voices the words he types.
MARTIN: This is called THE GRID it is standard programme but I customised it.
VO: No one thought Martin would ever speak, much less that he would find love.
His wife, Joanna, recalls it being a slow romance as Martin was still finding his voice when they first met in person.
JOANNA: he was using an alphabet board, so he had to spell everything, pointing... laughing.... But you know if you’re so in love you look at the eyes, not the alphabet boards, so it’s difficult to follow.
VO: Today he’s a successful web-developer in the UK. But, the life Martin now leads was once an impossible dream.
His book, Ghost Boy, reflects on his inspirational journey which started in Pretoria in the late eighties. Growing up Martin was a normal healthy boy curious about the world around him.
JOAN: Martin was so fine, could walk, he could run, he did everything a normal child could do, it was quite sad when he got ill.

VO: In 1988, at the age of 12, he began losing control of his muscles. His parents, Joan and Rodney watched their bright, active son become locked into his body.

JOAN: he wasn’t capable, he was too weak, he was like a baby, he couldn’t do anything (CRIES)....and after living with such a normal, happy, in fact he was such a clever child, I know most parents say that about their child, but he really was. He just deteriorated into nothing.

LINK: After a string of tests by doctors and specialists, there were still no answers – Martin had gone beyond what medicine understood.

RODNEY: We consulted all sorts of people. Spent 18 months in hospitals.
JOAN: They Initially thought it might be psychological, but they then decided after numerous tests, they then decided it must be a medical problem.

VO: Martin was screened for a range of neuro-degenerative diseases. He tested positive for crypto-coccal meningitis and tuberculosis of the brain – but there were no effective treatments.

Gradually, Martin slipped into a vegetative state and for the next four years switched off from the world around him.

Then at the age of 16, he began regaining consciousness - but no one noticed.

MARTIN: I often say it was like being a ghost, which is why the title of the book is Ghost Boy. //You can hear, see and understand everything around you but you have absolutely no power over anything. // every single thing in your life is decided by someone else.

LINK: Just imagine you can’t move, you can’t speak you are literally a prisoner inside your own body, it could be your worst nightmare, for Martin a cruel reality.

MARTIN: I was trapped inside my body, but no one knew I was alive. It is like you don’t exist. I know this may sound strange, but I often felt the presence of God, like he was with me all the time

VO: Paralysed from 1992 for close to a decade, he was able only to move his eyes.

MARTIN: I would sometimes watch things move, whether it be how sunlight moved throughout the day. Or watching insects of some sort scurry about, but really I lived in my mind to the point where at times I was oblivious to the world around me.

VO: While Martin was locked in his own body - and left to watch endless episodes of Barney the purple dinosaur - the world moved rapidly into the modern age with advances in technology like cellphones and the internet.

DEREK: You must have just seen life passing you by?
MARTIN: there were a number of major events that took place. // for example, The shock and sadness, when diana princess of wales died, and the nine eleven attacks on America. the excitement of Nelson Mandela being sworn in as president of south Africa, and the 1995 rugby world cup. // in a way I wasn’t part of it, I was a disconnected, detached observer.

VO: But not always: he can remember shocking treatment at the hands of primary care-givers who looked after him at various care centres in South Africa.

MARTIN: I was physically and verbally abused by a number of people through the years. Being abused does something to you, it changes something inside of you.

VO: In Martin’s book he describes his distraught mother being at his bedside.

Mum looked up at me. Her eyes were filled with tears. ‘You must die,’ she said slowly as she looked at me. ‘You have to die.’

JOAN: it’s true, I did say to him that I wished he died....
MARTIN: I am not angry or resentful or anything in fact I feel enormous compassion for my mum because it was a really hard time for her. // I was upset by it of course, but // I think what also upset me, especially with all the guilt I was already feeling wasn’t as much that she said that, but because we were in a situation where she felt that everyone would be better off if I wasn’t alive.
DEREK: Did you ever want to end it all – did you ever feel life is worth living?
MARTIN: many times I felt everyone, including myself would be better off if I were dead. In my book, I talk about the night I even tried to end my own life. But I didn’t even have the power to do that.

VO: His mum, Joan, also tried to commit suicide during those dark days.

JOAN: it was horrible, I just couldn’t handle it. After I’d taken what ever I took, I went to say goodbye to the family, and Rod said to me: “what have taken?” and they rushed me off to hospital.

VO: A night Martin remembers vividly.

MARTIN: To see and hear everything that was said, all the trauma caused, and real consequences that it had on everyone, and to know that I am the cause of it, I found really hard.

LINK: So was there a turning point, a magic moment, well it seems that there was and it was about a very perceptive therapist and the blink of an eye.

MARTIN: To actually become visible again, It was really exciting, // I think being seen, and having another person validate your existence is incredibly important, //

VO: In 2001 Martin’s therapist brought him to Pretoria University’s Centre for Alternative and Augmentative Communication - to evaluate his ability to communicate.

Professor Juan Bornman was part of the team that first assessed Martin.

PROF: Martin really had very limited forms of movement, and very limited forms of communication, so he came in a wheelchair, there was still a lot of tremor present in both his arms, and we actually could see at that stage already, this beautiful smile that he had. And that was the first communication attempts that we saw.

LINK: We all tend to look for a magic wand, but Martin got involved with here at the centre is a process to find a voice, at times a very different voice.

PROF: Having a disability like Martin’s does not present as a neat little thing that would fit into one little box.//

VO: Martin tried a range of devices from alphabet boards to symbol systems, but he was keen on finding a way to really speak again. His mum Joan took on the task of helping Martin master such a system.

DEREK: What do you appreciate most about being able to communicate again?
MARTIN: The power that it gives you and to be able to express your thoughts and personality.
PROF: Communication is really the essence of life, communication is what makes us human. INT 2 M4

VO: But for Martin, meeting wife Joanna meant finding the final missing piece.

MARTIN: Meeting Joanna changed my life. not only is she my soul mate but she supports, encourages and believes in me. She makes me want to be the best I can be, and always says to never let barriers stop me.

VO: The couple met during a Skype session with Martin’s Sister who lived in the UK. Their relationship developed over months of online chats.

His dad says Martin was head over heels in love from the beginning.

RODNEY: He used to spend hours on the computer communicating with each other.

VO: Martin’s parents believe Joanna’s kindness and love helped Martin become the man he is today.
RODNEY: One of the things we noticed when he Joanna got together was her ability to motivate him to actually improve
DEREK: DO you know what the amazing thing is? You’ve got a husband that has improved with age.
JOANNA: Yes! That’s true, like a good wine

VO: Writing the book was also part of the healing process. But for Joanna, reliving Martin’s epic journey was painful.

JOANNA: Here’s this guy, I love him and some how I need to discover this awful darkness that he had in his life and I felt sad, even angry and frustrated about it.

VO: Despite the darkness he faced, Martin believes his journey has universal lessons.

MARTIN: Never underestimate the power and importance of communication. And also to Treat everyone with kindness, dignity, compassion and respect, whether you think they understand or not.

PROMO 1
JOAN: he wasn’t capable, he was too weak, he was like a baby,

VO: Trapped in his body for almost a decade, Martin Pisturious breaks free.

PROMO 2

VO: Best-selling author Martin Pistorius as he takes us into the nightmare of a decade spent trapped in his own body, unable to speak or move.

MARTIN: To actually become visible again // having another person validate your existence is incredibly important.


PROMO 3 –

VO: Ghost Boy author, Martin Pistorius reveals his decade spent paralysed and with no one suspecting that he was fully conscious and aware.

MARTIN: For me, that feeling of complete and utter powerlessness is probably the worst feeling I have ever experienced, and I hope, I never have to experience again.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We speak to Martin Pistorius about his book and his journey to break free from a virtual coma that trapped him in his body for 12 years.
metadata.Summary: Martin Pistorius was a twelve-year-old boy in South Africa when he was struck by a mysterious illness. He was slowly debilitated... until he could no longer move his body, or speak. Then he slipped into what doctors called a vegetative state. His parents were told he would soon be dead. But after four years, something happened inside Martin. His mind began to function again, but not his body. He was soon fully aware of everything around him, but had no way of sharing. He was trapped inside his own body, like a ghost boy. But that's far from the end of Martin Pistorius's story. Because today, Martin is speaking again -- albeit with the help of a computer program.
metadata.Further information: Martin Pistorius book, Ghost Boy is taking the world by storm - it's been on the New York Times best Seller list for the last three weeks! He is currently in South AFrica visiting his family and has agreed to do an interview with Carte Blanche. Because he speaks through a computer, an interview is quite difficult as we have to provide questions beforehand so there isn't really a natural flow for pick up questions. I suggest that we include the Centre that helped Martin find his "voice". The Centre for Augmentative and Alternative Communication at the University of Pretoria did the initial tests on Martin and proved that he was in fact not in a vegetative state. If it weren't for the centre Martin would still be trapped, living out his years in a care centre watching Barney the Purple Dinosaur. DEVICE - we can use abstract re-enactments to help tell his story.
